chunks: Design a high-side PFET drive. The question: Design a circuit to properly drive a high-side PFET. Why is this needed?
To switch a high-voltage load with a PFET from a 3. 3 volts pin, you build a small circuit around its gate.
A small NFET, driven by the pin, pulls the PFET's gate down through a resistor. A pull-up resistor from gate to source keeps the PFET off by default.
A Zener diode (one that conducts above a set voltage) from gate to source stops the gate being pulled too far. It switches slowly, so it suits on/off load switching and slow PWM.
Think of a window blind with a pull cord, a spring and a stopper. The spring (pull-up resistor) keeps the blind closed. A person (the NFET) tugs the cord to open it.
The stopper (Zener) prevents tugging so far that the cord breaks. When the person lets go, the spring closes it again.
Spring and tug are both gentle, so the blind moves slowly: slow switching and heat.
With Q2 off, R gs holds the PFET gate at the bus: V GS equals 0 , off. With Q2 on, R c pulls the gate node down until the Zener clamps V GS at minus 12 volts.
The Zener's cathode is on the source (bus) side. Q2 is a low-side switch exactly like "Drive an inductive load from a GPIO", with a gate resistor and a pulldown.
D fw gives the motor current a path (anode at ground) when Q1 turns off.
Level-shifting NFET: a small transistor, source at ground, that the pin turns on to pull the PFET gate down.
R c : the resistor between that NFET and the PFET gate; it sets turn-on speed and standing current. R gs : the gate-to-source pull-up that holds the PFET off.
Gate Zener: clamps V GS at about -12 volts when on. Standing current: current that flows the whole time the switch is on.
Take a 48 volts bus, a 5 amps motor and a 3. 3 volts pin. With the pin low, the NFET is off and R gs holds the gate at 48 volts, so the PFET is off.
With the pin high, the NFET pulls the gate node down until the 12 volts Zener clamps it at 36 volts, so V GS equals -12 volts.
The standing current is (48 minus 12) over 10 k equals 3. 6 milliamps, which dissipates about 130 milliwatts in R c .
The gate time constant is 10 k times 2 nanofarads equals 20 microseconds, so this is fine near 1 kilohertz and poor beyond. That is the whole idea.
"PFET source on the bus, drain to the load.
A small 100 volts NFET level shifter, driven from the GPIO through a series resistor with a pulldown, pulls the PFET gate down through a 10 k resistor.
A 10 k pull-up from gate to source holds the PFET off, and a 12 volts Zener from gate to source clamps V GS so it can't exceed the rating at any supply voltage.
That gives about minus 12 volts of V GS when on and 0 when off, with 3. 6 milliamps standing current at 48 volts.
It's fine up to about 1 kilohertz; beyond that add a push-pull stage."
